'''Nancy Fern Olivieri''' (born 1954) is a prominent [[Toronto]] [[haematologist]] and researcher with an interest in the treatment of [[haemoglobinopathies]]. She is best known for a protracted struggle with the [[The Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto|Hospital for Sick Children]] and the [[pharmaceutical companies|pharmaceutical company]] [[Apotex]] about the drug [[deferiprone]].<ref name=viens>{{cite journal |vauthors=Viens A, Savulescu J | title = Introduction to The Olivieri symposium. | journal = J Med Ethics | volume = 30 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–7 | year = 2004 | pmid = 14872065 |url= | doi = 10.1136/jme.2003.006577 | pmc = 1757126}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Olivieri was born to the [[Hamilton, Ontario]], Doctor Fernando Olivieri and Victoria Olivieri.<ref name=spec>{{cite web|url=https://www.thespec.com/news-story/2146017--uncle-red-barton-street-s-kid-doctor/|title='Uncle Red': Barton Street's kid doctor|publisher=thespec.com|date=August 21, 2011|access-date=August 6, 2019|archive-date=August 6, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190806180948/https://www.thespec.com/news-story/2146017--uncle-red-barton-street-s-kid-doctor/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Her paternal grandfather had immigrated to Hamilton from Italy in 1909.<ref name=spec/> Olivieri received a Bachelor of Science from the [[University of Toronto]] and an MD from [[McMaster University]] in 1978.<ref name=creds>{{cite web|url=https://ims.utoronto.ca/faculty/faculty-online-community/faculty-members/olivierinancy/|title=Nancy Olivieri - Institute of Medical Science - University of Toronto|publisher=ims.utoronto.ca|access-date=2019-08-06|archive-date=2019-08-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190806180948/https://ims.utoronto.ca/faculty/faculty-online-community/faculty-members/olivierinancy/|url-status=dead}}</ref> She has also pursued training in Internal Medicine and Hematology at McMaster, University of Toronto, and [[Harvard University]].<ref name=creds/>

==Deferiprone controversy==
Starting in 1989, Olivieri was part of a group evaluating the use of a drug, [[deferiprone]], in treating persons with the blood disorder [[thalassaemia]].<ref name=viens/> Starting from 1985, this work included a clinical trial partly funded by Apotex.  During the course of the trial, Olivieri became concerned about evidence that pointed to the drug being inefficacious for some patients. Olivieri informed both the research ethics board that was monitoring the study and Apotex, the drug maker. The research ethics board instructed Olivieri to inform participants about her concerns. Apotex responded by noting that Olivieri had signed a confidentiality agreement as part of the drug trial and that informing participants about her concerns, the validity of which Apotex disputed, would violate that confidentiality agreement. In 1996, Apotex threatened to vigorously pursue legal remedies against her if she disclosed her conclusions to patients.<ref name=viens/> Olivieri disclosed her concerns to her patients, and Apotex ended the portion of the study in which she was participating. In 1998, the ''[[New England Journal of Medicine]]'' published a paper by Olivieri and seven other authors, with further study results suggesting that [[deferiprone]] led to progressive [[hepatic fibrosis]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1056/NEJM199808133390701  |vauthors=Olivieri NF, Brittenham GM, McLaren CE, etal |title= Long-term safety and effectiveness of iron chelation therapy with oral deferiprone in patients with thalassemia major.  |journal= N. Engl. J. Med. |volume=339 |issue=7 |pages=417–428 |year=1998 |pmid=9700174|doi-access=free }} [http://content.nejm.org/cgi/content/full/339/7/417?ijkey=8a83e2997b6b0b8d1f10d0f93152177c7aac3e70 Full Text] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120708221606/http://content.nejm.org/cgi/content/full/339/7/417?ijkey=8a83e2997b6b0b8d1f10d0f93152177c7aac3e70 |date=2012-07-08 }}.</ref><ref name=textbook>{{cite book |last1=Hadskis |first1=Michael |editor1-first=Jocelyn |editor1-last=Downie |others=et al. |title=Canadian Health Law and Policy |type=textbook |edition=Third |year=2007 |publisher=LexisNexis |page=304 |chapter=The Regulation of Human Biomedical research in Canada}}</ref>

Olivieri's scientific findings, which sparked the controversy, have been challenged on the basis of data from clinical trials conducted by Apotex.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=M.A. Tanner, MRCP |author2=R. Galanello, MD |author3=C. Dessi, MD |author4=G.C. Smith, MSc |author5=M.A. Westwood, MD |author6=A. Agus, MD |author7=M. Roughton, MSc |author8=R. Assomull, MRCP |author9=S.V. Nair, MRCP |author10=J.M. Walker, MD |author11=D.J. Pennell, MD |title=A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Double-Blind Trial of the Effect of Combined Therapy With Deferoxamine and Deferiprone on Myocardial Iron in Thalassemia Major Using Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance |journal=Circulation |volume=115 |pages=1876–1884 |year=2007 |doi=10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.106.648790 |pmid=17372174 |issue=14|doi-access=free }} [http://circ.ahajournals.org/cgi/content/full/115/14/1876 Full Text].</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite journal |vauthors=Brittenham G, Nathan D, Olivieri N, Porter J, Pippard M, Vichinsky E, Weatherall D |title=Deferiprone and hepatic fibrosis |journal=Blood |volume=101 |issue=12 |pages=5089–90; author reply 5090–1 |year=2003 |pmid=12788794 |doi=10.1182/blood-2002-10-3173|doi-access=free }} [http://www.bloodjournal.org/cgi/content/full/101/12/5089 Full Text].</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Wanless I, Sweeney G, Dhillon A, Guido M, Piga A, Galanello R, Gamberini M, Schwartz E, Cohen A |title=Lack of progressive hepatic fibrosis during long-term therapy with deferiprone in subjects with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia |journal=Blood |volume=100 |issue=5 |pages=1566–9 |year=2002 |pmid=12176871 |doi=10.1182/blood-2002-01-0306|doi-access=free }} [http://www.bloodjournal.org/cgi/content/full/100/5/1566 Full Text].</ref>

[[Deferiprone]] is approved for use in over 50 countries, but not in [[Canada]].<ref name="savulescu">{{cite journal |author=Savulescu J |title=Thalassaemia major: the murky story of deferiprone |journal=BMJ |volume=328 |issue=7436 |pages=358–9 |year=2004 |pmid=14962851 |doi=10.1136/bmj.328.7436.358 |pmc=341373}} [http://www.bmj.com/cgi/content/full/328/7436/358 Full Text].</ref>  It was approved in the US in 2011 under the FDA's accelerated approval program.<ref>FDA NEWS RELEASE: FDA Approves Ferripox (deferiprone) to Treat Patients with Excess Iron in the Body, Oct. 14, 2011 [https://web.archive.org/web/20111016005918/http://www.fda.gov/NewsEvents/Newsroom/PressAnnouncements/ucm275814.htm]</ref>

An investigation commissioned by the [[Canadian Association of University Teachers]] (CAUT) revealed that one of Olivieri's critics, [[Gideon Koren]], had anonymously sent disparaging letters about Olivieri to the media and colleagues. Koren initially denied responsibility, but substantial DNA evidence tied him to the letters, and he was reprimanded.<ref name=CAUT>{{citation |author1=Jon Thompson |author2=Patricia Baird |author3=Jocelyn Downie |title=Report of the Committee of Inquiry on the Case Involving Dr. Nancy Olivieri, the Hospital for Sick Children, the University of Toronto, and Apotex Inc. |url=http://www.caut.ca/docs/af-reports-indepedent-committees-of-inquiry/the-olivieri-report.pdf?sfvrsn=0 |publisher=www.caut.ca |access-date=8 December 2015 |archive-date=13 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230113181545/https://www.caut.ca/docs/af-reports-indepedent-committees-of-inquiry/the-olivieri-report.pdf?sfvrsn=0 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Olivieri has advocated greater [[academic freedom]] and called for less control of research by [[Pharmaceutical industry|pharmaceutical companies]].<ref>{{cite journal | author = Olivieri N | title = Patients' health or company profits? The commercialisation of academic research | journal = Sci Eng Ethics | volume = 9 | issue = 1 | pages = 29–41 | year = 2003 | pmid = 12645227 | doi = 10.1007/s11948-003-0017-x| s2cid = 32796175 }}</ref> This situation was publicised extensively and was investigated by the Canadian Association of University Teachers.<ref name=CAUT/>

==Awards and honours==
Olivieri was awarded the 2009 [[AAAS Award for Scientific Freedom and Responsibility]] for her ''"indefatigable determination that patient safety and research integrity come before institutional and commercial interests and for her courage in defending these principles in the face of severe consequences."''<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aaas.org/aboutaaas/awards/freedom/freedom2009.shtml |title=AAAS - Award for Scientific Freedom and Responsibility - 2009 Award Recipient |access-date=2010-11-22 |archive-date=2013-05-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515204926/http://www.aaas.org/aboutaaas/awards/freedom/freedom2009.shtml |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Olivieri is the 2023 recipient of the [[John Maddox Prize]] in recognition of her ''“determination to act with integrity…in the face of extreme pressure from the company producing it, ultimately at great personal cost”'' in the Deferiprone controversy.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cressey |first1=Daniel |title=Scientists honoured for facing down lawsuits to reveal findings |date=25 October 2023 |url=https://www.researchprofessionalnews.com/rr-news-world-2023-10-scientists-honoured-for-facing-down-lawsuits-to-reveal-findings/ |publisher=Research Professional News |access-date=25 October 2023}}</ref> The Maddox Prize is awarded by the UK-based [[Sense about Science]] charity in partnership with [[Nature (journal)]].
